--- layout: dilemma permalink: /dilemmas/care-ethics-for-and-about/ title: "Caring For and Caring About" summary: "You can care for the person in front of you, or care about many people you will never meet." ---

Every Tuesday evening you volunteer-tutor a child in your neighborhood. The child is not doing well in school, and they are not easy to help, but over a few years of volunteering you have learned more about how they think, when they shut down, what makes them try again, etc.

For the sake of this example, if you stop coming to tutor this child, no one else is going to take the volunteer hour.

One week you are informed that the same volunteer hours given to a famine relief organization would do more measurable good. By volunteering in the organization's warehouse, you will support more lives for more years and prevent more suffering. You will never meet the children, they will never know your name, and you will never see their response.

Again, for the sake of this example, you cannot do both, and you must decide...

What should be done?

Context: Nel Noddings, whose work founded much of modern care ethics, drew a distinction between caring for and caring about. Caring for is a relationship which requires a real-world encounter. Caring about is what we do for people at a distance, by sending money or feeling concern. Noddings argued that we are not obligated to care for suffering children/people in distant places in the same way we are obligated to care for those near us.

This is possibly one of the most debated claims in care ethics. Critics argue it permits comfortable people to continue enabling suffering simply because they are distant from it and never see it.

Source: Nel Noddings, Caring: A Feminine Approach to Ethics and Moral Education (University of California Press, 1984); reissued as Caring: A Relational Approach to Ethics and Moral Education (2013).

Source: Maureen Sander-Staudt, "Care Ethics", The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy — obligations to proximate versus distant others.

See also: Joan Tronto, Moral Boundaries: A Political Argument for an Ethic of Care (Routledge, 1993) - on "privileged irresponsibility."

See also: Peter Singer, "Famine, Affluence, and Morality", Philosophy & Public Affairs 1, no. 3 (1972): 229–243 — argument that distance from suffering makes no difference.
